shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Poland's GDP per capita, PPP, as % of Spain's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Fifty-five dollars. {p} That's the gap this year between the average Spaniard and the average Pole: income per person, adjusted for prices. About sixty thousand dollars each, and Spain is ahead by fifty-five. Ninety-nine point nine percent. {pp} In 1990, Poland was at forty-two percent of Spain. Half by 2006. Seventy percent in 2012. Ninety in 2020. {p} And next year, in the IMF's forecast, Poland passes Spain. By 2031, it's nine percent ahead.

In this series, Poland has passed Japan, and it's closing in on Britain and France. Spain is the next one to actually fall. {p} And here's what makes it interesting: Spain isn't stuck. Its economy is one of the fastest-growing big economies in Europe right now. Poland is passing it anyway. {pp} <soft>Here's how Spain got caught, the two crashes that did it, and what passing Spain really means, and doesn't.</soft>

Quick one before the chart: this is a series, and the next episode is Italy, the big economy Poland is closest to catching after Spain: about six thousand dollars behind this year. Subscribe so you don't miss it. {p} Now, the race.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Poland's GDP per capita, PPP, as % of Spain's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: In 1990, the average Spaniard produced about sixteen thousand dollars a year, adjusted for prices. The average Pole, about six thousand seven hundred. {p} Since then, Poland's economy has grown about three and a half times, after inflation. Spain's has doubled. When Poland joined the European Union in 2004, it was still at forty-nine percent: just under half. {pp} But the line didn't rise smoothly. It moved fastest in two moments, and both were Spanish crashes: after 2008, and in 2020.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth, Spain (annual %); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Here's Spain's economy, year by year, after inflation. {p} First crash: after 2008, Spain shrank in four different years, 2009, 2011, 2012 and 2013. By 2013, the economy was about eight percent smaller than in 2007, and unemployment hit twenty-six percent. {pp} Second crash: 2020. Minus eleven percent, one of the deepest falls in Europe that year, with tourism shut down. Poland's was about minus two. In that single year, Poland jumped from eighty-two percent of Spain to ninety-three.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth (NGDP_RPCH), population (LP), unemployment (LUR)
shots.title: Growing, but sharing it
shots.narration: Since then, Spain has bounced back hard: almost four percent growth in 2024, and about two and a half last year and this year. {p} But there's a catch for income per person: people. Spain's population has grown from about thirty-nine million in 1990 to almost fifty million, mostly through immigration. Poland's has shrunk to about thirty-six. {pp} So even when Spain's economy grows fast, it's shared between more people every year. And from 2027, the IMF has Spain slowing to under two percent, and Poland holding at two and a half.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ (NGDPDPC); inflation (PCPIPCH)
shots.title: Where Spain still wins
shots.narration: Now, what passing Spain doesn't mean. {p} In plain dollars, without adjusting for prices, the average Spaniard produces about forty-two thousand dollars this year, and the average Pole about thirty-one thousand. There, Poland is at seventy-five percent, and still at about eighty-four in 2031. Even so, that gap has collapsed: in 1990, in plain dollars, the average Spaniard produced more than eight times as much as the average Pole. In 2004, almost four times. Now, about one point three. {pp} So a Spanish salary still buys more in euros. What changes is this: measured by what money actually buys at home, the average Pole is now as well off as the average Spaniard. {p} And on inflation, Spain did better in 2022: about eight percent, against Poland's fourteen.
And if you're enjoying the series, the subscribe button is right there. Italy is next. {p} Now, where Poland already wins.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · unemployment rate (% of labor force), 2026 estimate
shots.title: Unemployment, 2026
shots.narration: Unemployment this year: about three point two percent in Poland, {pp} nine point eight in Spain. Three times as high. And government debt: about sixty-seven percent of the economy in Poland, about ninety-eight in Spain. {p} Spain's unemployment has been higher than Poland's every single year since 2008. In 2013, at the bottom, it was twenty-six percent in Spain, and about ten in Poland.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · PPPPC (GDP per capita, PPP, current international $); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.title: The pass
shots.narration: So here's the pass, in the IMF's numbers. {p} This year: Spain sixty thousand one hundred and six dollars, Poland sixty thousand and fifty-one. Fifty-five dollars apart. {p} Next year: Poland about sixty-three thousand six hundred, Spain about sixty-two thousand five hundred. Poland ahead by about eleven hundred. {pp} And by 2031, about six thousand two hundred ahead. For comparison: in 2010, Spain was about twelve thousand dollars ahead.

stats.at: sixty thousand one hundred and six
stats.label: Spain, 2026

shots.narration: For a lot of Poles, Spain was the dream holiday, and for many, a place to move for work. In 1990, the average Spaniard was more than twice as well off as the average Pole. {p} Next year, by this measure, that's over. One caveat: these are IMF estimates and forecasts, and a gap of fifty-five dollars can flip either way with one revision. But the trend has pointed the same way for thirty-five years. {p} If you're Polish and you go to Spain on holiday, prices there will still look higher than at home. That's the plain-dollar gap. What's gone is the gap in what people can afford in their own country.

<soft>So, your guess: does Poland actually pass Spain next year, or does the revision go the other way?</soft> Tell me in the comments. {p} If you're watching from Spain: does this match what you see? {p} If you're in Poland: did you expect this moment to come so soon? {p} And Italy: you're next. I read every comment.
And if you missed it, France is the next big one after Spain: eighty-seven percent, and a date around 2031. That story is right here. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Poland Is $55 Behind Spain. Next Year, It Passes.
yt.description:
Income per person, adjusted for prices (IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026): Poland was 42% of Spain in 1990, half in 2006, 90% in 2020 and 99.9% this year — $60,051 vs $60,106, a $55 gap. In the IMF's forecast Poland passes Spain in 2027 and is ~9% ahead by 2031. Spain's two crashes (2008–2013 and 2020), why fast Spanish growth is shared by more people, where Spain still wins (plain dollars: Poland 75%; 2022 inflation) and where Poland wins (unemployment 3.2% vs 9.8%, debt).

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 (PPPPC, NGDPDPC, NGDP_RPCH, LP, LUR, GGXWDG_NGDP, PCPIPCH). 2026+ figures are IMF estimates and forecasts.
